papers.title: DAT-SPECT findings in POLR3A-related striatal variant: a case report and literature review.
papers.abstract: The POLR3A striatal variant manifests with prominent extrapyramidal signs, ranging from early-onset dyskinetic syndromes to juvenile parkinsonism. This case report offers the first DAT SPECT evidence of nigrostriatal involvement, revealing significant reductions in striatal binding and decreased putamen-to-caudate ratios. These findings provide preliminary in vivo functional evidence of presynaptic dopaminergic involvement, offering a valuable biological correlate for the clinical phenotype.

papers.title: An examination of the effect of dual task on gait in Parkinson's disease and REM sleep behavior disorder.
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND: Gait variability is a hallmark of Parkinson's disease (PD) and has been linked to cognitive deficits and fall risk. Rapid eye movement sleep behavior disorder (RBD) is a strong predictor of synucleinopathies, yet evidence for gait changes in RBD is inconsistent. Performing a dual task increases gait variability, an effect that can be quantified using a cost function. OBJECTIVE: Determine the degree to which dual task cost differs between control, RBD, and PD participants at baseline, and between RBD converters versus non-converters at follow-up. METHODS: 46 RBD, 23 control, and 14 PD participants completed standardized gait analysis at baseline. Parameters chosen a priori for analysis included enhanced gait variability index (eGVI), functional ambulation performance (FAP), velocity, step length, cadence, base of support, and double support time. Medical records were surveilled for 3 years following participant enrollment, determining that 6 RBD participants converted to Parkinsonism. Baseline gait indices and dual task costs were compared between control, RBD, and PD groups at enrollment, and between RBD stable and RBD converters at follow-up. RESULTS: The PD group had greater eGVI, as well as greater dual task cost for FAP, cadence, width, and double support time. No differences in gait variability or cost were identified between RBD and control groups at baseline. Compared to the stable group, RBD converters had greater dual task cost for FAP, velocity, cadence, and double support time. CONCLUSIONS: Increases in dual task cost for specific gait parameters may identify RBD patients at imminent risk of phenoconversion.

papers.title: A Data-Driven Operational Definition of Square-Wave Jerks and Its Diagnostic Utility in Progressive Supranuclear Palsy.
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND: The Movement Disorder Society diagnostic criteria for progressive supranuclear palsy (PSP) list frequent square-wave jerks (SWJ) as a suggestive oculomotor feature. A standardised operational definition of SWJ is however presently lacking. OBJECTIVE: To create a data-driven optimal SWJ definition and to assess its diagnostic utility in PSP. METHODS: We prospectively recruited PSP n = 25, Parkinson's disease (PD) n = 32, Alzheimer's disease (AD) n = 35, and controls n = 88. SWJ were recorded with a visual fixation task using video-oculography. Multiple candidate definitions of SWJ were generated by systematically varying morphological features, producing 32 candidate definitions. A nested cross-validation was used to obtain unbiased diagnostic performance and optimised SWJ definition. Results were then externally tested in a fully independent sample of n = 25 PSP, n = 41 PD and n = 25 controls. RESULTS: The optimal selected SWJ definition consisted of saccade amplitude 1°-8°, intra-SWJ intervals 20-600 ms, directional opposition within ±45°, and amplitude similarity ≤ 0.25. Only SWJ rate, and not morphological features, was distinctive for PSP. SWJ rate gave out-of-fold AUCs of 0.81 for PSP versus controls, 0.71 for PSP versus AD, 0.63 for PSP versus PD, and 0.76 for PSP versus all non-PSP groups. Post hoc analyses using this data-driven definition on the external validation cohort yielded relatively comparable results. SWJ rate > 24/min had high specificity, but low sensitivity, for PSP when compared with PD. CONCLUSIONS: SWJ rate was significantly increased in PSP but with insufficient discriminant ability for use as a stand-alone diagnostic marker. This data-driven definition may serve as a reproducible operational definition for future research.

papers.title: Parkinson's Disease-Associated Genetic Alterations Disrupt Behavior and Diurnal Activity in Drosophila melanogaster.
papers.abstract: Parkinson's disease (PD) is a progressive neurodegenerative disorder characterized by the loss of dopaminergic neurons, resulting in motor dysfunction and a variety of non-motor symptoms. Multiple genetic alterations, including increased α-synuclein expression and loss-of-function of parkin, PINK1, and DJ-1, have been associated with PD pathogenesis; however, their effects on stress tolerance, motor behavior, and daily activity remain incompletely understood. This study investigated the effects of PD-associated genetic alterations on stress tolerance, motor behavior, and diurnal activity in Drosophila melanogaster. Four Drosophila lines representing PARK1 (SNCA/α-synuclein; elav-GAL4>UAS-hSNCA), PARK2 (PRKN/parkin; parkinⁿᵘˡˡ), PARK6 (PINK1; PINK1ᴮ⁹), and PARK7 (DJ-1; DJ-1βΔ⁹³) were evaluated using assays of starvation survival, larval vertical migration, adult negative geotaxis, jumping activity, and locomotor activity under a 12h light:12h dark cycle. Starvation stress tolerance differed among PD-associated fly lines in males and females separately. All PD-associated fly lines exhibited impaired larval vertical migration, whereas adult negative geotaxis and jumping behavior showed genotype-dependent patterns, with no significant genotype × sex interaction. Activity monitoring revealed disruptions in daily locomotor activity, with visually observed alterations in morning and evening activity patterns. Daily activity patterns also showed clear sex-specific differences. These findings show that PD-associated genetic alterations affect stress tolerance, locomotor behavior, and diurnal activity in D. melanogaster, with the nature of these effects varying by genotype, sex, and behavioral phenotype. papers.title: Dysregulated cholesterol trafficking through ABCA1 drives neurodegeneration in Parkinson's disease.
papers.abstract: Although brain cholesterol dysregulation is implicated in Parkinson's disease (PD), targeting cholesterol synthesis has shown limited efficacy. Here we identify ATP-binding cassette transporter A1 (ABCA1) as a critical regulator of cholesterol homeostasis in PD. We show that ABCA1 expression is elevated in the substantia nigra of postmortem PD brains and in a PD mouse model, with regional analyses revealing preferential alterations in nigral and striatal circuits. Mechanistically, astrocytic ABCA1 drives excessive cholesterol efflux in mice, promoting neuronal cholesterol overload. In neurons, ABCA1 localizes to lysosomes, where it facilitates cholesterol import, leading to cholesterol accumulation, autophagy impairment and α-synuclein pathology. Genetic silencing of Abca1 in either astrocytes or dopaminergic neurons attenuates neurodegeneration and behavioral deficits in vivo. Furthermore, we identify magnesium citrate as an ABCA1 inhibitor and show that it reduces dopaminergic neuronal loss in a PD mouse model. Our findings identify an ABCA1-dependent cholesterol pathway underlying PD pathogenesis and support ABCA1 inhibition as a potential disease-modifying strategy.

papers.title: The Role of Astrocytes in the Inflammatory Response in Neurodiseases.
papers.abstract: Astrocytes have emerged as central regulators of neuroinflammation, extending far beyond their traditional roles as structural and metabolic support cells. In neurological disorders, astrocytes undergo reactive remodeling that encompasses morphological, transcriptional, metabolic, and functional changes. Rather than fitting into a fixed A1/A2 dichotomy, reactive astrocytes exist along a disease-, region-, and stage-dependent continuum shaped by local pathology and intercellular crosstalk. This review summarizes how astrocytes contribute to neuroinflammatory processes in Alzheimer's disease, Parkinson's disease, amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, Huntington's disease, central nervous system injury, infection, multiple sclerosis, epilepsy, and autism spectrum disorder. We highlight convergent mechanisms, including cytokine and chemokine release, complement activation, glutamate and ion homeostasis disruption, oxidative stress, metabolic reprogramming, and blood-brain barrier regulation, while emphasizing disease-specific astrocytic programs. We further discuss astrocyte interactions with microglia, neurons, oligodendrocytes, endothelial cells, and peripheral immune cells, as well as key regulatory pathways, epigenetic remodeling, and lipid-dependent metabolic signaling. Finally, we evaluate current and emerging astrocyte-targeted therapeutic strategies, including metabolic modulation, receptor targeting, gene editing, nanodelivery, and gut-brain axis interventions. Defining functionally validated astrocyte states and developing biomarker-guided, stage-adaptive therapies may enable more precise intervention in neuroinflammatory and neurodegenerative diseases.

papers.title: Cerebrospinal fluid and dural accumulation of α-synuclein impairs CNS clearance in Parkinson's disease.
papers.abstract: Parkinson's disease (PD) is characterized by the build-up of α-synuclein (α-syn) in the brain, where it drives neurodegeneration. Importantly, aggregated α-syn also accumulates in the cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) of PD patients, and while increasingly used for diagnosis, its pathological role remains poorly understood. Here, we demonstrate that α-syn accumulation in central nervous system (CNS) border tissues promotes CNS clearance deficits, as observed in PD patients. We find that aggregated α-syn accumulates not only in the CSF but also in the dura mater of individuals with PD, and, using acute and chronic mouse models, show that α-syn deposition in these sites induces immune alterations in CNS borders and disrupts CNS clearance. Mechanistically, we reveal that α-syn at CNS borders elevates CSF TNF and demonstrate that both TNF and α-syn aggregates themselves impair lymphatic endothelial cell function. These findings demonstrate a pathological role for α-syn in the CNS border tissues and position meningeal immunity as a contributor to CNS clearance deficits in PD pathogenesis.

papers.title: The efficacy of psychological interventions for anxiety in Parkinson's disease: a systematic review and meta-analysis including mindfulness and mind-body approaches.
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND: Anxiety is a prevalent and clinically significant non-motor symptom in individuals with Parkinson's disease (PD), yet the overall efficacy of psychological interventions for anxiety in this population remains unclear. This meta-analysis aimed to evaluate the effectiveness of psychological and mind-body interventions in reducing anxiety symptoms among individuals with PD and to explore potential differences according to theoretical orientation. METHODS: Randomized controlled trials (RCTs) examining psychological or mind-body interventions reporting anxiety outcomes in individuals with PD were systematically identified in four databases searched to 27 July 2026. Effect sizes were calculated as standardized mean differences using Hedges' g within a random-effects model, with between-study variance estimated by restricted maximum likelihood and inference based on the Hartung-Knapp adjustment. Heterogeneity was assessed using Cochran's Q and I² statistics, and a prediction interval was calculated. Subgroup analyses compared cognitive-behavioral and interpersonal therapies with mindfulness- and mind-body-based approaches, and active with inactive control conditions. Sensitivity analyses, including leave-one-out procedures and exclusion of trials at high risk of bias, were performed. Publication bias was examined using funnel plot inspection and Egger's regression test, and the certainty of evidence with GRADE. RESULTS: Across 13 comparisons from 13 trials and 877 participants, psychological and mind-body interventions were associated with a statistically significant reduction in anxiety symptoms (Hedges' g = - 0.46, 95% CI [- 0.67, - 0.25]). Heterogeneity was moderate (I² = 40.7%, 95% CI 0% to 79%), and the 95% prediction interval, - 1.00 to + 0.08, included the null. papers.title: Effect of Different Cortical Targets of Transcranial Magnetic Stimulation on Freezing of Gait in Parkinsonism: A Systematic Review.
papers.journal: Physiotherapy research international : the journal for researchers and clinicians in physical therapy
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND AND PURPOSE: Freezing of gait (FOG) is a disabling and episodic gait disturbance in patients with Parkinson's, with varying responses to noninvasive brain stimulation. Transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) has been explored as a therapeutic option; however, the optimal cortical target for reducing FOG remains unclear. This systematic review synthesizes and critically evaluates the available evidence regarding the effects of TMS applied to different cortical targets on FOG-related outcomes, with emphasis on the indirect nature of comparisons between targets. METHODS: A systematic search was conducted in four electronic databases (PubMed, Cochrane Library, Web of Science, and Scopus) from inception to December 2025, followed by an updated search conducted through July 21, 2026. Randomized and crossover randomized controlled trials investigating the effects of TMS on FOG in parkinsonism were included. Studies have used TMS with a variety of protocols to target different cortical regions. They evaluated FOG-related outcomes by using validated questionnaires or objective tasks. Risk of bias was assessed using the Cochrane Risk of Bias 2 tool. Because of heterogeneity in stimulation protocols and outcome measures, a narrative synthesis was performed. RESULTS: The updated search identified additional records; however, no new eligible studies were identified after screening. Therefore, ten studies met the inclusion criteria. Favorable FOG-related findings were reported in some studies targeting the primary motor cortex, including reductions in Freezing of Gait Questionnaire scores and improvements in gait performance, with effects persisting for several weeks in some studies. Findings regarding stimulation of the supplementary motor area were variable, ranging from reported reductions in FOG-related outcomes to limited effects and, in one study, worsening of gait performance. papers.title: Time To Stable Programming After Staged vs Simultaneous Bilateral Subthalamic Deep Brain Stimulation Electrode Placement for Parkinson's Disease.
papers.abstract: OBJECTIVE: To compare programming visits and time to stable stimulation and medication management after staged versus simultaneous bilateral subthalamic nucleus deep brain stimulation (DBS) for Parkinson's disease. METHODS: This retrospective study included the original selected cohort of 10 staged and 10 simultaneous bilateral DBS patients, matched during cohort selection by age, disease duration, and surgical year. Continuous and count variables were summarized as medians and interquartile ranges (IQRs). Groups were compared using exact permutation Mann-Whitney tests and Fisher's exact test, as appropriate. RESULTS: The simultaneous group required fewer programming visits than the staged group (median 3 [IQR 3-5] vs 7.5 [IQR 6-10], P < 0.001) and had a shorter interval from initial implantation to stable therapy (5.5 [IQR 3-7] vs 14.5 [IQR 12-17] months, P = 0.007). An exploratory comparison of recorded levodopa equivalent dose reduction did not detect a difference between groups (P = 0.905). CONCLUSIONS: In this small retrospective cohort, simultaneous implantation was associated with fewer programming visits and a shorter overall interval to stable bilateral therapy. The timing difference includes the interval between staged procedures and does not establish superior clinical efficacy or equivalent medication outcomes.

papers.title: The Pallidothalamic Tract in Functional Neurosurgery: A Systematic Review.
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND: The pallidothalamic tract (PTT), formed by convergence of the ansa lenticularis and fasciculus lenticularis at Forel's field H1, is a major basal ganglia efferent pathway and an emerging functional neurosurgical target. No systematic review has previously synthesised outcomes across PTT-targeted interventions. METHODS: This PRISMA 2020-compliant systematic review was registered on PROSPERO (CRD420251248260). PubMed, OVID, and Web of Science were searched for studies reporting functional neurosurgical outcomes targeting the PTT or Forel's fields. Prospective and retrospective studies, case series, and case reports were eligible. Methodological quality was assessed using design-appropriate risk-of-bias tools. RESULTS: Forty studies encompassing 483 patients (1966-2025) were included across five modalities: MR-guided focused ultrasound (n=143), radiofrequency ablation (n=167), deep brain stimulation (n=40), cryogenic lesioning (n=82), and oil-wax injection (n=52). Mean follow-up was 21 months. In Parkinson disease (11 studies; n=135), mean UPDRS-III improvement was 39%, with reductions in dyskinesia (UDysRS 90%) and tremor (75%). In dystonia (12 studies; n=87), BFMDRS and TWSTRS improved by 57% and 47%, respectively. Dual-target strategies, particularly PTT-VIM combinations, showed additive effects, including greater tremor reduction (77%) and improved rigidity. In drug-resistant epilepsy (6 studies; n=157), seizure reduction occurred in 71% and seizure freedom in 33%. CONCLUSIONS: PTT-targeted interventions yield meaningful motor improvements in Parkinson disease and dystonia, with preliminary evidence supporting additive dual-target benefits. Seizure-reducing effects in refractory epilepsy have been reported. Evidence remains limited by small uncontrolled studies, heterogeneous outcomes, and inconsistent adverse-event reporting. Prospective trials will elucidate the efficacy, safety, and clinical role of the PTT in neurosurgery.

papers.title: Parkinson's disease LRRK2 mutations dysregulate iron homeostasis and promote oxidative stress and ferroptosis in human neurons and astrocytes.
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND: Iron accumulation is a hallmark of sporadic and familial Parkinson's disease (PD) and correlates with clinical motor symptom severity. The biochemical mechanisms driving iron dyshomeostasis in PD brain and whether these are early or late events in the neurodegenerative process remain unknown. Nigral iron levels in LRRK2-PD patients have been reported to be even higher than in idiopathic PD, and greater in non-manifesting LRRK2 carriers than controls, suggesting that iron accumulation precedes clinical onset in LRRK2-associated PD. However, the cells affected and mechanisms governing iron dyshomeostasis in PD remain unclear. METHODS: Here, we investigated multiple independent measures of iron homeostasis in human iPSCs and iPSC-derived models, including glutamatergic and dopaminergic neurons, and astrocytes, carrying pathogenic LRRK2 mutations. High-content and super-resolution microscopy of iron-specific probes and ICP-MS were used to determine iron content and distribution across different cell types and LRRK2 genotypes. Upstream effectors and downstream consequences of iron dyshomeostasis, including oxidative stress and ferroptosis-related phenotypes were also examined. RESULTS: Pathogenic heterozygous LRRK2 mutations were associated with altered iron homeostasis across multiple human cell models. Lysosomal ferrous iron was consistently elevated across iPSC-derived glutamatergic neurons, dopaminergic neurons, and astrocytes carrying LRRK2 mutations and these phenotypes were reduced by varying degrees following treatment with the selective LRRK2 inhibitor, MLi-2. Importantly, we show that lipid peroxidation and ROS levels are elevated in isogenic LRRK2 mutant neurons, while iron chelation or MLi-2 reduced LRRK2-dependent ROS damage. papers.title: ClC-7 links PIKfyve inhibition to Rab-dependent LRRK2 activity at lysosomes.
papers.abstract: Increased activity of leucine-rich repeat kinase 2 (LRRK2) confers Parkinson's disease risk. LRRK2 dynamically localizes to lysosomal membranes in response to various stresses, yet the mechanisms by which distinct lysosomal perturbations are communicated to LRRK2 remain unclear. Here, we show that inhibition of the lysosomal lipid kinase PIKfyve promotes LRRK2 recruitment and signaling through a pathway that requires the lysosomal chloride/proton antiporter ClC-7. ClC-7 in turn controls the accumulation of multiple Rab GTPases on lysosomes. LRRK2 signaling under these conditions requires its established Rab-binding surfaces, with Rab12 contributing significantly to this response. This pathway operates independently of CASM. In contrast, lysosomal stresses that induce CASM require both Rab-binding sites on LRRK2 and GABARAP for robust LRRK2 signaling. These findings identify ClC-7-dependent lysosomal remodeling and Rab accumulation as key features linking PIKfyve inhibition to LRRK2 signaling and reveal that distinct lysosomal stresses engage different combinations of Rab and GABARAP inputs to activate LRRK2.

papers.title: Swollen lysosomes grab Rabs for a CASM-free route to LRRK2 activation.
papers.abstract: Multiple lysosomal stresses activate Parkinson's-linked LRRK2 kinase, and these involve the so-called "CASM" pathway to help recruit LRRK2 to lysosome surfaces. Clegg et al. (https://doi.org/10.1083/jcb.202511137) show that LRRK2, activated upon lysosome swelling caused by PIKfyve inhibition, instead relies solely on Rab GTPase binding for lysosome localization and activation.
